title: Voiceless 'TH' Sound (as in 'Think', 'Cathedral', 'Through')
tongue_position: Place the tip of your tongue gently between your upper and lower front teeth (or just behind the edge of your top teeth). Do not clamp down.
lip_shape: Relax your lips and keep them slightly open.
airflow: Blow a continuous, gentle stream of air over the tongue tip. No vocal cord vibration (unvoiced). It should sound like soft friction.
common_pitfall: Replacing /θ/ with /s/, /t/, or /f/ (saying 'sink' or 'tink' instead of 'think').
practice_drill: The author thought through three thrilling theories.

title: Voiced 'TH' Sound (as in 'The', 'That', 'Rhythm')
tongue_position: Same tongue placement as /θ/ (tip between upper and lower teeth), but activate your voice box.
airflow: Continuous airflow with vocal cords buzzing. Touch your throat: you should feel a distinct vibration.
common_pitfall: Replacing /ð/ with /d/ or /z/ (saying 'de' or 'ze' instead of 'the').
practice_drill: These brothers and their father gather together smoothly.

title: Distinguishing 'S' and 'SH' (as in 'Seashells', 'She')
tongue_position: For /s/: Tongue tip points close to the roof just behind upper front teeth (alveolar ridge). For /ʃ/ (sh): Pull tongue slightly further back, blade of tongue arched toward the palate.
lip_shape: For /s/: Wide, smiling lips. For /ʃ/: Flare lips forward in a slight trumpet or pout shape.
airflow: Sharp, hissing jet of air down the tongue center for /s/. Broader, softer whooshing sound for /ʃ/.
common_pitfall: Collapsing both sounds into /s/ or /sh/ (e.g. saying 'see-sells' or 'she-shells' for 'seashells').
practice_drill: She sells shiny seashells by the silent seashore.

title: Liquid Consonants: American 'R' vs 'L' (as in 'Right', 'Light')
tongue_position: For /r/: Tongue curls or bunches backward in the mouth; the tongue tip NEVER touches the roof of your mouth. For /l/: Tongue tip presses firmly against the alveolar ridge behind top teeth, letting air flow out the sides.
lip_shape: For /r/: Slightly rounded lips. For /l/: Neutral lips.
airflow: Voiced air resonates through the oral cavity for /r/. Lateral airflow past the sides of the tongue for /l/.
common_pitfall: Flapping the tongue tip against the roof of the mouth for /r/ (producing a flap /d/ or /l/).
practice_drill: Red lorries and yellow lorries roll rapidly along the road.

title: Labiodental 'V' vs Bilabial 'W' (as in 'Very', 'Wary', 'Wednesday')
tongue_position: For /v/: Tongue stays neutral in floor of mouth. For /w/: Back of the tongue raises toward the soft palate.
lip_shape: For /v/: Upper front teeth rest lightly on inside of the LOWER lip. For /w/: Both lips form a tight circle (like whistling or sipping through a straw), with teeth NOT touching lips.
airflow: For /v/: Voiced friction between top teeth and bottom lip. For /w/: Voiced smooth glide through rounded lips.
common_pitfall: Using /w/ for /v/ ('wery' for 'very') or touching teeth to lips for /w/.
practice_drill: We viewed very vast wetlands on Wednesday.

title: Aspirated Plosive 'P' (as in 'Peter', 'Piper', 'Picked', 'Peck')
lip_shape: Press both lips firmly together to build up air pressure in the mouth.
airflow: Release lips abruptly with a crisp puff of air (aspiration). If you hold a tissue before your mouth, it should visibly flutter.
common_pitfall: Unaspirated or weak 'p' that sounds like 'b'.
practice_drill: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers promptly.

title: Silent Letters & Tricky English Spelling
tongue_position: Skip the silent consonant entirely; transition your tongue directly from the preceding vowel to the following consonant.
lip_shape: Follow the vowel shape, do not close lips for silent 'b' or 'w'.
airflow: Continuous voicing across the syllable transition.
common_pitfall: Pronouncing silent 'b' in 'subtle' (/ˈsʌt.əl/, NOT sub-tul), silent 'd' in 'Wednesday' (/ˈwɛnz.deɪ/, NOT wed-nes-day), or saying /tʃ/ for 'choir' (/ˈkwaɪ.ər/, NOT choy-er).
practice_drill: The subtle choir on Wednesday sang without a doubt.

title: Multi-Syllable Stress & Cadence
tongue_position: Open vowels on stressed syllables; reduce unstressed vowels to the neutral schwa /ə/ (tongue relaxed in center).
lip_shape: Pronounce stressed syllables with greater jaw opening and longer duration.
airflow: Higher pitch, increased vocal loudness, and elongated vowel duration on the stressed syllable.
common_pitfall: Pronouncing every syllable with equal weight and volume, making English sound robotic and hard to comprehend.
practice_drill: Clear pronunciation builds confidence during professional conversations.
